newsitem.title: UK: Dollar Eurobonds ride the crest of a wave.
newsitem.headline: Dollar Eurobonds ride the crest of a wave.

text.p: Like the hidden fifth card in a stud poker game, U.S. jobs data announced last Friday turned out to be a winner for U.S. Treasuries and dollar assets generally in an already buoyant dollar Eurobond market.

Dealers said the market had been holding four key cards -- a positive dollar story, high absolute yields, large upcoming redemptions and political confusion in Europe over EMU -- and saw issuance surge as a result.
Then the jobs report for May revealed the lowest jobless rate for 23 years alongside a slowing rate of employment growth, thus reducing expectations of another U.S. interest rate hike.
"As long as a deal is correctly priced there's hardly a cloud on the horizon at the moment," said a Eurobond syndicate manager at a U.S. bank here.
International dollar bonds totalling around $15 billion were launched last week, bringing the total for the year to just above $150 billion.

Deals included billion-dollar offerings from the Asian Development bank, Ford and Toyota. Denmark, the European Investment Bank and a host of other top-rated names issued smaller, but still sizeable, bonds.
Players expected issuance to continue apace with top-notch Japanese names to the fore as well as a jumbo global deal for German Bayerische Landesbank.

Names like Japan Highway, JFM and Tokyo were mooted. All tap the Euromarket on a regular, almost clockwork, basis and their time is due. BayerLB has been the subject of talk about a $1.0 billion 10-year offering.
European buyers of such paper should have few currency worries, dealers said, with the dollar within a couple of pfennigs of three-year highs against the mark.

Analysts said international politics favoured further improvement. Growing uncertainties in Europe about the timing of economic and monetary union was the main factor and thought of any slippage in the timetable would see a rush to the dollar as a safe haven, analysts said.
The German government and central bank have been sharply divided about plans to revalue the country's gold reserves to help meet EMU qualification criteria.
That crisis may be dwarfed after today's move by France to ask for time to consider the so-called stability pact designed to ensure spending discipline among countries inside EMU.
Financial markets have been wary of France since its recent surprise election of a socialist government.
Expectations of EMU starting on the January 1, 1999 deadline prescribed under European Union law, had led to long-term interest rate convergence in Europe over the past year or more.
This, syndicate managers said, has left long-dated U.S. rates at levels which are attractive to investors both in relative terms and and on an absolute basis.
A shake-out in U.S. Treasuries in late May took the long bond yield above 7.00 percent and the 10-year note above 6.75 percent.
These levels were a key event for investors who were then happy to buy the market on the belief it was unlikely to offer much better value in the near term.
In terms of relative value, the U.S. jobs figures saw the yield gap between 10-year U.S. and German government paper narrow six b.p. to just under 85 b.p,, its narrowest level for some while.
The spread was just shy of 120 b.p. as recently as mid-April and analysts looked for further U.S. outperformance.

Analysts said the slowing in May employment growth should bolster U.S. Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan's confidence "that the economy, in general, and consumer spending, in particular, will slow to a sustainable pace in coming quarters".
Dollar Eurobonds' final trump card was the level of dollar bond redemptions in coming months.

After international bonds worth $5.0 billion matured in May, the level rose to $9.3 billion in June and $16.3 billion in July, the biggest single month of redemptions of the year, according to Capital DATA Bondware.
